specPoints.text: understand, the following techniques in the preparation and purification of a liquid organic compound: i heating under reflux ii extraction with a solvent using a separating funnel iii distillation iv drying with an anhydrous salt v boiling temperature determination

primer.text: Turning a reaction mixture into a clean liquid takes three crafts: boiling without losing a drop, collecting only what boils where expected, and washing the water away. This note walks reflux, distillation and solvent extraction, including the boiling-point purity check and the drying agents that finish the job.

lessons.title: Heating under reflux keeps everything in the flask
lessons.opening: Many organic transformations crawl along at ambient temperature, so chemists heat the mixture for extended periods. Reflux is the arrangement that permits prolonged heating while trapping every volatile species, and this lesson walks the full apparatus recipe and names the reactions that rely on it.
keyPoints: Reflux allows slow organic reactions to be heated for long periods without losing reactants, products or solvent.
Reflux aims to retain every chemical in the vessel, unlike distillation which deliberately separates a component out.
Ester formation from an alcohol plus acid, and oxidising a primary alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid, are classic reflux reactions.
The condenser stands vertical, with cooling water entering at the bottom and leaving at the top, so vapours condense and drip back.
Anti-bumping granules encourage smooth boiling, and a heating mantle or water bath supplies the heat safely.

low.restatement: Reflux means boiling a reaction mixture while a vertical condenser turns escaping vapour back into liquid, so the vessel keeps its contents no matter how long the heating lasts.
low.analogy: Picture a lidded saucepan: steam hits the lid, drips back into the stew, and nothing boils dry no matter how long it simmers.
low.examPointer: Always contrast reflux with distillation in answers: reflux retains everything, distillation removes the volatile fraction, and quoting that contrast earns the mark.

medium.restatement: Vapour leaving the mixture meets a cold glass surface inside the water jacket and condenses; gravity returns the droplets to the flask, so the reaction can run for hours at its boiling point with zero loss of material.
medium.analogy: A climber on an escalator moving down while they walk up makes no net progress - the vapour climbs into the condenser and is carried straight back down as liquid.
medium.examPointer: Mention greased Quickfit joints, anti-bumping granules and water entering low and exiting high whenever a question asks you to describe the reflux set-up.

check.stem: Why is a reaction mixture heated under reflux rather than simply boiled in an open flask?

options.text: Reflux returns escaping vapour to the flask so nothing escapes during prolonged heating
options.explanation: The vertical condenser condenses vapour and returns it, letting the mixture boil for hours without loss.

options.text: Reflux raises the boiling point of the solvent above its normal value
options.explanation: The boiling point is a property of the liquid; the condenser changes nothing about it.

options.text: Reflux removes the volatile product as soon as it forms
options.explanation: That describes distillation; reflux is chosen precisely to keep volatile species in the vessel.

options.text: Reflux stops the mixture from boiling at all
options.explanation: The mixture does boil; the point is that escaping vapour is condensed back in.

check.stem: Which conversion is typically carried out by heating under reflux?

options.text: Oxidising a primary alcohol fully to a carboxylic acid
options.explanation: Complete oxidation needs prolonged heating with excess oxidising agent, the classic reflux job.

options.text: Separating two liquids with different boiling points
options.explanation: Separation by volatility is distillation, not reflux.

options.text: Washing an organic layer with sodium carbonate solution
options.explanation: That purification step happens in a separating funnel at room temperature.

options.text: Drying an organic liquid over anhydrous sulfate
options.explanation: Drying agents work in a stoppered flask, not in reflux apparatus.

check.stem: In the reflux set-up, cooling water flows through the condenser jacket so that

options.text: Water enters at the bottom and exits at the top, keeping the jacket full and the glass cold
options.explanation: Filling against gravity prevents air pockets, so the whole condenser surface stays cold for condensing vapour.

options.text: Water enters at the top and trickles down by gravity alone
options.explanation: Top-fed water leaves air gaps in the jacket and poor cooling.

options.text: Water circulates only when the mixture is left to cool afterwards
options.explanation: The water runs throughout the heating, not after it.

options.text: The water is heated to boiling so no condensation shock occurs
options.explanation: Cold water is what condenses the vapour; warming it would defeat the purpose.

check.stem: Anti-bumping granules are added to the reflux flask because they

options.text: Promote smooth, controlled boiling instead of violent bumping
options.explanation: The granules give nucleation sites so bubbles form steadily rather than explosively.

options.text: Act as a catalyst for the organic reaction
options.explanation: They are inert glassy material with no catalytic role.

options.text: Absorb any water produced during the reaction
options.explanation: Drying agents do that job; granules do not absorb anything.

options.text: Raise the reaction temperature beyond the solvent boiling point
options.explanation: Boiling occurs at the normal boiling point; granules do not change it.

check.stem: The ester ethyl ethanoate can be prepared by refluxing an alcohol with an acid. The role of the acid catalyst here is to

options.text: Speed the ester formation while the mixture boils safely under reflux
options.explanation: Acid catalysis accelerates esterification, and reflux lets the slow reaction run to completion without loss.

options.text: Neutralise the alcohol before reaction begins
options.explanation: The acid catalyses the reaction; it does not destroy the alcohol first.

options.text: Keep the condenser water cold during heating
options.explanation: Cooling water and the acid catalyst are unrelated.

options.text: Convert the ester back into the starting alcohol
options.explanation: Catalysts speed both forward and back reactions; the acid is not added to reverse anything.

check.stem: State the purpose of heating under reflux.
check.modelAnswer: Reflux heats a reaction for as long as needed while a condenser returns vapour to the flask, so no reactants, products or solvent are lost.

check.stem: Name two pieces of safety or practical equipment used in a reflux set-up besides the condenser.
check.modelAnswer: Anti-bumping granules to promote smooth boiling, and a heating mantle or water bath in place of a naked flame, plus greased Quickfit joints for a good seal.

check.stem: Explain why the condenser in reflux apparatus is clamped vertically rather than at an angle.
check.modelAnswer: A vertical condenser lets condensed vapour run straight back down into the flask by gravity, so nothing collects in the condenser and every volatile species returns to the reaction mixture.

check.stem: A student refluxes an alcohol with acidified potassium dichromate intending the carboxylic acid, but fits the condenser at a downward angle so distillate escapes. Predict the most likely product collected outside the flask and justify it.
check.modelAnswer: The aldehyde intermediate, which boils lower than the alcohol, escapes before it can be further oxidised in the flask, so the escaping distillate is enriched in aldehyde while full oxidation to the acid is lost.

lessons.title: Distillation separates by boiling point and reveals purity
lessons.opening: When a reaction stops short of completion or throws off unwanted co-products, distillation rescues the desired liquid. This lesson follows the apparatus from still head to receiver, explains the collection window around the expected boiling point, and uses boiling behaviour as a purity fingerprint.
keyPoints: Distillation separates components of a mixture by their different boiling points, the lowest boiling first.
Producing an aldehyde from a primary alcohol is a standard distillation, with the aldehyde boiling lower than the alcohol.
The thermometer bulb sits where vapour passes into the condenser so it reads the distilling vapour temperature.
Distillate is collected only within about two degrees of the expected boiling point; fractions outside are discarded.
A sharp, constant boiling point signals a pure liquid, while impurities spread boiling over a range and often raise it.

low.restatement: Heat the mixture, and whichever liquid boils first climbs over as vapour, condenses in the water-jacketed condenser and drips into the receiver; collecting only near the expected boiling point keeps the product clean.
low.analogy: Think of a race where the runners leave the stadium in order of their eagerness - the most volatile liquid leaves the flask first, just as the fastest runner exits first.
low.examPointer: Quote the two-degree collection window and the boiling-point purity argument together: both are standard exam credit points for organic preparation questions.

medium.restatement: The vapour temperature at the still head equals the boiling point of the component currently leaving; when that temperature holds steady near the literature value, the distillate is the wanted compound, and a drifting or elevated reading betrays impurities or a new fraction.
medium.analogy: A crowded bus empties passenger by passenger as each stop arrives; each component distils at its own boiling-point stop, one after another.
medium.examPointer: Explain the discarded forerun and the stopped collection when a question hands you a temperature range: below the window is contaminant, above it the wanted liquid has already all left.

check.stem: Why is distillation the technique of choice when a primary alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde?

options.text: The aldehyde boils lower than the alcohol, so it can be removed as soon as it forms
options.explanation: Distilling off the aldehyde protects it from the further oxidation that reflux would allow.

options.text: The aldehyde is denser than the reaction mixture and drains out
options.explanation: Density plays no role in distillation; volatility does.

options.text: The aldehyde reacts with the condenser water and must be removed quickly
options.explanation: The aldehyde is inert to the cooling water; it is collected because it is volatile.

options.text: Distillation speeds up the oxidation reaction itself
options.explanation: Distillation does not change the reaction rate; it separates the product.

check.stem: Where should the thermometer bulb sit in the distillation apparatus?

options.text: Level with the entrance to the condenser, where the vapour flows past it
options.explanation: The bulb must read the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser, which is the distilling component's boiling point.

options.text: Immersed deep in the boiling liquid in the flask
options.explanation: That reads the liquid temperature, not the vapour being collected.

options.text: At the top of the still head, far above the vapour path
options.explanation: Too high a position reads cooler room-affected air, not the vapour.

options.text: Inside the receiving vessel with the distillate
options.explanation: The collected liquid has already cooled, so the reading would be meaningless.

check.stem: A distillate fraction comes over well below the expected boiling point. What should be done with it?

options.text: Discard it and collect a fresh fraction once the temperature reaches the expected window
options.explanation: Early low-boiling material is contaminant, so the receiver is changed before the wanted fraction arrives.

options.text: Keep it, because all distillate is the desired product
options.explanation: Mixing fractions contaminates the product with lower-boiling impurities.

options.text: Heat the fraction further to raise it to the expected boiling point
options.explanation: A pure liquid boils where it boils; heating collected liquid does not relocate it into the window.

options.text: Redistil it immediately at a higher temperature
options.explanation: The standard practice is to discard the forerun and collect the window fraction cleanly.

check.stem: What does a sample that boils over a range of temperatures indicate?

options.text: The liquid is impure, since impurities spread and usually raise the boiling temperature
options.explanation: A pure liquid boils sharply at one temperature; a spread of boiling betrays contamination.

options.text: The liquid is pure but its boiling point is unstable
options.explanation: Boiling points are reproducible for pure liquids; instability is not a thing here.

options.text: The thermometer was placed in the boiling liquid
options.explanation: Even a correct placement would still show a sharp value for a pure liquid.

options.text: The condenser water was flowing too fast
options.explanation: Cooling rate affects condensation, not the boiling range of the sample.

check.stem: Electric heating mantles are preferred over Bunsen burners for distilling organic liquids because

options.text: The temperature is controllable and the flammable vapours meet no naked flame
options.explanation: Organic liquids ignite easily, so a flame-free, adjustable heat source is the safe choice.

options.text: Bunsen burners cannot reach the boiling points of organic liquids
options.explanation: A Bunsen flame is hot enough; the problem is ignition risk, not temperature reach.

options.text: Mantles condense the vapour more efficiently than burners
options.explanation: Condensation is the condenser's job, not the heater's.

options.text: Mantles stir the mixture automatically during heating
options.explanation: Heating mantles provide heat only; stirring is separate.

check.stem: State how distillation separates the components of a mixture.
check.modelAnswer: The mixture is heated and each component distils at its own boiling point, the lowest boiling liquid leaving first and condensing in the condenser.

check.stem: Define the collection window used when distilling a desired product.
check.modelAnswer: Distillate is collected only within about two degrees of the expected boiling point; material arriving below or above that window is discarded.

check.stem: Explain why boiling point determination can be used as evidence of both identity and purity.
check.modelAnswer: Every pure liquid boils at a characteristic temperature that can be matched against literature values for identity, and impurities shift and spread that temperature, so a sharp value at the literature boiling point demonstrates purity too.

check.stem: An oxidation of a primary alcohol is left to reflux by mistake instead of being distilled. The flask contents are then distilled and a fraction arrives at the alcohol's boiling point. Identify that fraction and explain its presence.
check.modelAnswer: Unreacted alcohol: the extended reflux drove oxidation past the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid, so when the mixture is finally distilled the first volatile fraction is acid-related and the alcohol comes over near its own boiling point only after the lower-boiling species have left.

lessons.title: Washing, separating and drying the organic product
sourceHeadings: Solvent extraction / use of a Separating Funnel
lessons.opening: A freshly made organic liquid rarely leaves the reaction clean. Water rides along with it, acidic residues need neutralising, and traces of moisture must go before the product is stored. This lesson covers the separating-funnel wash routine and the anhydrous salts that finish the drying.
keyPoints: Water formed or used in a reaction usually forms an aqueous layer beneath the organic layer in a separating funnel.
Adding a little water and watching which layer grows identifies the aqueous layer when the two look alike.
Sodium carbonate solution neutralises acidic residues and washes out other impurities before separation.
The funnel is stoppered, inverted and vented through the stopcock repeatedly to release built-up pressure.
Anhydrous salts such as calcium chloride or magnesium sulfate hydrate to remove remaining traces of water; clumping means more drying agent is needed.

low.restatement: Swirl the crude organic liquid with aqueous reagent in a separating funnel, vent often, let the layers split, drain the aqueous layer away, then swirl the organic layer with an anhydrous salt until the salt stays powdery - the liquid is then dry and can be decanted.
low.analogy: It is like washing salad then patting it dry: the rinse removes the dirt, and the absorbent towel takes the last of the water off the leaves.
low.examPointer: Name the diagnostic tests in answers: the layer that grows on adding water is aqueous, and a drying agent that clumps signals water still present.

medium.restatement: Neutralisation with carbonate releases carbon dioxide, which is why the stopcock is opened slowly and venting repeated; the anhydrous salt binds water into its own crystal lattice as a hydrate, so a fine powder floating freely means no free water remains for it to bind.
medium.analogy: Rice in a damp salt cellar clumps while it soaks up moisture and flows freely once the cellar is dry - the drying agent behaves the same way.
medium.examPointer: State that calcium chloride suits hydrocarbons while magnesium or calcium sulfate are general-purpose, and that the dry liquid is decanted or filtered off the solid.

check.stem: After an organic preparation, the separating funnel holds two colourless layers. How do you identify the aqueous layer?

options.text: Add a little water and see which layer increases in volume
options.explanation: The added water joins the aqueous layer, so the layer that grows is the water-rich one.

options.text: Warm the funnel gently and watch which layer evaporates
options.explanation: Heating a stoppered funnel is unsafe and does not identify layers.

options.text: Assume the top layer is always aqueous
options.explanation: Aqueous layers are often but not always lower; density decides, and the test removes the guesswork.

options.text: Taste a drop of each layer
options.explanation: Laboratory chemicals are never tasted; this is both forbidden and unreliable.

check.stem: Sodium carbonate solution is added to a separating funnel containing a crude ester in order to

options.text: Neutralise acidic impurities and remove them by washing
options.explanation: The carbonate reacts with acid residues, releasing carbon dioxide, leaving the organic layer cleaner.

options.text: Act as a drying agent for dissolved water
options.explanation: Anhydrous salts dry the liquid; carbonate solution is itself aqueous and adds water.

options.text: Catalyse further ester formation
options.explanation: No esterification is intended during washing; the carbonate cleans the product.

options.text: Dissolve the organic product for re-extraction
options.explanation: The organic product stays in its own layer; the carbonate washes the impurities away.

check.stem: Why must the stopcock of a separating funnel be opened periodically during shaking?

options.text: To release pressure built up by gases such as carbon dioxide from neutralisation or vaporisation
options.explanation: Trapped pressure would force the stopper out and eject the contents when the funnel is inverted.

options.text: To let air in so the liquids mix better
options.explanation: Mixing is achieved by shaking; venting is about pressure, not aeration.

options.text: To allow the layers to separate faster
options.explanation: Separation happens on standing; venting does not accelerate it.

options.text: To check the colour of the organic layer
options.explanation: Observation is done through the glass, not by opening the tap.

check.stem: Anhydrous calcium chloride is added to a damp organic liquid. Continued clumping of the solid tells you that

options.text: Water is still present, so more drying agent is needed until some powder stays dispersed
options.explanation: Clumps form as the salt hydrates; free-flowing leftover powder proves the liquid is dry.

options.text: The drying is complete and the liquid can be decanted at once
options.explanation: Clumping signals the opposite - drying is not finished.

options.text: The calcium chloride has catalysed an unwanted reaction
options.explanation: The salt simply binds water; clumping is a hydration sign, not a reaction.

options.text: The organic liquid has dissolved all of the drying agent
options.explanation: Drying agents are chosen for low solubility; clumping is hydration, not dissolution.

check.stem: Which drying agent is the usual choice for drying a hydrocarbon product?

options.text: Anhydrous calcium chloride
options.explanation: Calcium chloride is the standard hydrocarbon dryer; the sulfates serve as general-purpose agents.

options.text: Sodium carbonate solution
options.explanation: That is an aqueous washing reagent, the opposite of a drying agent.

options.text: Concentrated sulfuric acid
options.explanation: It would react with or char many organics; it is not a drying agent here.

options.text: Damp silica gel
options.explanation: Damp material adds water; drying agents must be anhydrous.

check.stem: State how a drying agent removes water from an organic liquid.
check.modelAnswer: The anhydrous salt hydrates, binding traces of water into its own solid structure, and is then removed by decanting or filtering the dry liquid.

check.stem: Outline the separating-funnel procedure used to wash an organic product.
check.modelAnswer: Transfer the mixture to the funnel, stopper, invert and vent via the stopcock repeatedly, let the layers separate, then drain the aqueous layer off so the organic layer can be collected.

check.stem: Explain why an organic layer usually sits above an aqueous layer in a separating funnel.
check.modelAnswer: Most organic liquids are less dense than water, so the aqueous layer sinks below the organic layer; the water-addition test confirms which is which whenever the densities are less certain.

check.stem: A crude ester smells of acid after washing. Suggest the residual impurity, the reagent that removes it, and the observation that confirms the removal is under way.
check.modelAnswer: Residual acid impurity; sodium carbonate solution removes it by neutralisation, confirmed by fizzing carbon dioxide released each time the funnel is vented through the stopcock.

glossary.definition: Continuous boiling of a reaction mixture with a vertical condenser returning vapour to the flask so nothing is lost during prolonged heating.
Separation of liquids by boiling point, collecting the vapour of the lowest boiling component as it condenses.
An anhydrous salt that binds residual water by hydrating, added until some powder stays freely dispersed in the organic liquid.
Vessel used to wash crude organic products and drain off the aqueous layer after the layers separate.
